note: Daily practice after the 28-day course: 9 modules of 10 days. Education about communication, not legal advice or therapy.

days.title: The clean expense ask
chat: Welcome to daily practice. The 28 days are done, and from here it's one real-life topic at a time.
First up is money. Money texts go wrong when the past rides along with the amount.
The clean version has four parts: what it was, what it cost, their share, and the receipt.
Nothing about who paid last time. That's a different conversation, and usually not one for text.

them: hey did u ever send the dentist $ or

options.text: not yet, sending my $85 half on venmo tonight. thx for the reminder
options.why: It answers with the amount and a time, so there's nothing left to ask.

options.text: pretty sure i sent it? i'll check my venmo at some point this week when things calm down
options.why: It sounds calm but gives no amount and no day, so the question stays open.

options.text: 3 wks lol. u took 2 months to pay for the cleats so
options.why: It drags up an old debt and starts a scorekeeping fight.

days.tryToday: Send one expense text today with just the item, the amount, their share and a photo of the receipt.

days.title: When they won't pay their half
chat: Sometimes you send the clean ask and they just say no.
It's tempting to argue fairness. By text that almost never moves anyone.
Restate the amount once, say when you'd like it, and point to what you both agreed if there is something written.
Then stop. You don't have to win the argument to keep a clear record of the ask.
replies: What if they still say no?

them: u signed her up not me

options.text: fine, forget it. i'll just cover all of it like always, it's honestly easier than asking u
options.why: It gives up the ask and adds a sigh they can grab onto.

options.text: wow ok. remember this next time u want me to split something
options.why: It's a threat to get even later, and it keeps the fight going.

options.text: we talked about karate on 3/2 and u said yes. ur half is $45, by the 15th?
options.why: It points to the date you agreed, names the amount and asks for a day.

days.tryToday: If someone owes you a share, send one message with the amount, the date you agreed and a pay-by day.

days.title: When they ask for receipts
chat: Being asked for receipts can feel like being called a liar.
Try to read it as a normal ask. Sending the receipt is the fastest way to end the thread.
No need to say you're offended. Just send the photo.

them: before i send anything i need to see receipts
not just ur word for it this time

options.text: omg seriously? u think i'm making up a $30 field trip??
options.why: It turns a normal ask into a fight about trust.

options.text: sure, sending photos of all 3 receipts now. total's $112, ur half is $56
options.why: It just sends the proof and the math, which ends it.

options.text: i'll dig them up when i have time, things have been crazy
options.why: It's calm but vague, so the money keeps waiting and so does the thread.

days.tryToday: Start a phone folder or album just for kid receipts and put today's in it.

days.title: "Must be nice" texts
chat: Some money texts aren't about a bill at all. They're about how your life looks from the outside.
"Must be nice" is bait. There's nothing in it to answer.
You can skip it, or answer only the part that's about the kids.

them: meanwhile caleb needs new shoes and i guess thats on me

options.text: i'll grab caleb's shoes this wknd. what size is he now?
options.why: It skips the truck and answers the one thing about the kids.

options.text: i've been saving 2 years for that truck fyi, it's not like i'm rich
options.why: It defends a purchase that wasn't really the question.

options.text: yeah it is nice actually. maybe get a better job
options.why: It takes the bait and adds a new insult to fight about.

days.tryToday: Next time a money jab comes in, find the one line about the kids and answer only that.

days.title: The support payment that's late
chat: When a payment is late, the first text sets the tone for the whole week.
If it's on your side, say when it's going out. If it's on theirs, ask once with a date.
Skip the guesses about why. They feel like accusations even when you mean them kindly.

options.text: ugh my bank does this, not my fault, they always hold transfers for like 3 days for no reason
options.why: It explains and blames the bank, but never says when the money lands.

options.text: it's literally been 1 day. relax
options.why: It brushes off the worry and invites a sharper reply.

options.text: i'll check w/ the bank today and text u by 5 when it's sent
options.why: It gives a next step and a time, which is what they need before Friday.

days.tryToday: If a payment of yours is ever late, practise the line: what happened, and when it'll land.

days.title: Expenses you didn't agree to
chat: Sometimes the bill comes after the decision. They signed the kid up, then sent you half.
You can be fair without saying yes to everything.
Say what you can pay, and ask to talk first next time. Calm, short, no lecture.

them: travel team is 1200 for the season

options.text: ok i'll make it work, i'll send the 600 by monday
options.why: It agrees to a big cost you never discussed, which sets up the next one too.

options.text: i can do $300 by monday. next time can we decide on big stuff like this first?
options.why: It offers a clear amount and asks for a heads-up next time.

options.text: lmao u signed him up without asking and want me to pay half? no
options.why: It's heated and a flat no, with no option on the table.

days.tryToday: Before the next big cost comes up, send a one-line ask: can we agree on anything over a set amount before signing up?

days.title: Saying no to a cost
chat: A no doesn't need five reasons. One reason and one option is plenty.
The more reasons you give, the more they have to argue with.
Say no, say why in a few words, and offer something you can do.

them: ava wants the new iphone for her bday
shes the only one in her class w/o one ngl

options.text: i don't think she needs one. phones are bad for kids her age, i read this article that said
options.why: It turns a no into a debate about phones that won't end.

options.text: ok sure, if everyone has one i guess we should
options.why: It says yes to something you don't want, just to avoid the push.

options.text: not a phone this year for me. i'm happy to split a gift up to $100 tho
options.why: It's a short no with one option, so there's a next step.

days.tryToday: Say no to one thing this week in two sentences or fewer, with one thing you can offer.

days.title: Lost and broken stuff
chat: Coats, tablets, retainers. Things go missing between two homes, and someone has to replace them.
The fight is usually about whose fault it was. That one is hard to settle.
What usually works is solving the next step: who looks, who buys, and by when.

them: it was in his bag when he left MY house

options.text: i'll check the car and his room tonight. if it's not here, can we split the new one?
options.why: It looks first, then offers a fair split, with no blame either way.

options.text: ok, i'll pay the whole $250, my bad
options.why: It takes the blame and the full cost before anyone has even looked.

options.text: well it wasn't in his bag when he got here, i unpacked it myself, so it must be at ur place
options.why: It's calm but just pushes the blame back, which stalls everything.

days.tryToday: Make a quick list of the things that travel between homes, so a missing one is easy to check.

days.title: Money talk near the kids
chat: Kids notice money stress, and they hear it when it gets sent through them.
"Tell your dad to pay for your shoes" puts a kid in the middle of an adult bill.
If a money message comes through a kid, answer the adult directly and leave the kid out of it.
replies: What do I say to my kid?

them: mia said u told her u cant afford her dance recital fee
why would u say that to her

options.text: i didn't say that, she must've heard wrong. she exaggerates
options.why: It calls the kid unreliable and argues about what was said.

options.text: i'll talk w/ mia tonight so she's not worried. the recital fee is covered, i'll send it fri
options.why: It settles the kid's worry and the money, and nothing else.

options.text: ok well maybe if support was on time she wouldn't have to hear it
options.why: It's a polite-sounding dig that turns the kid's worry into a money fight.

days.tryToday: Notice one time this week you're about to mention money near the kids, and save it for later.

days.title: Settling up once a month
chat: One way to cut down on money fights is to have fewer money texts.
Some parents settle up once a month: one message, every item, one total.
It's not a rule, just a habit that gives the topic a regular, boring home.
That's the money module done. Tomorrow starts schedule changes.

them: can we just do all the kid money at once
im sick of 10 venmo requests a week tbh

options.text: it's not 10 a week, it's like 3 at most. i only send stuff i actually spend money on
options.why: It argues the count and misses that they're agreeing with you.

options.text: whatever's easiest for u, i'm flexible
options.why: It sounds easy but sets no day, so nothing changes.

options.text: yeah good idea. i'll send one list w/ receipts on the 1st of each month?
options.why: It says yes and names the day, so there's a plan.

days.tryToday: Pick a day each month and write it down as your settle-up day.

days.title: The last-minute swap
chat: This module is schedule changes. They're the most common co-parenting text there is.
A last-minute swap ask is just a question. Yes, no, or yes with a change.
Answer it with the day and time spelled out, so there's no "I thought you meant" later.

them: can u take them thurs instead of fri

options.text: yes, i'll grab them thursday from school at 3 and have them till sat at 10
options.why: It says yes with the day, the time and when they come back.

options.text: sure np, i can probably do thursday, just text me when u know more about ur work thing
options.why: It's friendly, but nobody knows the pickup time or when they go back.

options.text: again?? that's the 3rd time this month
options.why: It counts their swaps instead of answering, and it's heated.

days.tryToday: Confirm your next schedule change with the day, the time and who drives, all in one message.

days.title: When they're late again
chat: You're in the lot. They're 25 minutes late. Your phone is right there.
The text you send in that moment tends to be the one you'd most like to take back.
Ask for the one thing you need: when they'll get there. Save the pattern for your record, not the thread.

options.text: it's ALWAYS traffic w/ u. every single time
options.why: It's an always about the past, and it starts round two.

options.text: ok no rush at all, take ur time, we'll just hang out here in the lot for however long it takes
options.why: It sounds kind but tells them late is fine, which isn't true for you.

options.text: ok. i'll wait till 5:45, after that i'll take them home and u can grab them there
options.why: It sets a clear limit and a backup plan, without a lecture.

days.tryToday: Next time someone's late, write the time down for yourself and keep the text to the next step.

days.title: When you're the one running late
chat: It happens to everyone. The text you send when you're late matters more than the lateness.
Send it early, give a real time, and skip the long story.
One short apology is fine when you're actually late. Five lines of reasons is not.

options.text: sorry sorry, my boss kept me, then the gas light came on, then the bridge was
options.why: The long story reads like excuses and still gives no arrival time.

options.text: sorry, running late. i'll be there at 6:25
options.why: It owns it in one word and gives a real time.

options.text: 10 min chill, u were late last week
options.why: It's late and keeping score, which makes them madder.

days.tryToday: If you're ever running late, text before the time, not after, with when you'll arrive.

days.title: Saying no to a swap
chat: You're allowed to say no to a swap. A schedule only works if it's mostly kept.
A kind no is short: no, maybe one reason, and an option if you have one.
No guilt paragraph needed.

them: hey any chance u could keep jayden next wknd too

options.text: i can't next wknd, i have plans. i could do sat till 2 if that helps?
options.why: It's a clear no with one small option.

options.text: ugh ok fine, i'll move my stuff around
options.why: It says yes when you mean no, and you'll resent it.

options.text: i'm sorry, it's just that i already told my friend and work is crazy and i'd feel bad if
options.why: It over-explains, which gives them lots to argue with.

days.tryToday: Say no to one ask this week in two short sentences, with an option if you have one.

days.title: The no-show
chat: They didn't come and they didn't text. Your kid is at the window.
One calm message asking about the plan is enough. Chasing with five texts doesn't bring them faster.
Then turn your attention to your kid. They need you more than the thread does.
replies: What do I tell my kid?

options.text: tell her urself. she's been waiting by the door for an hour
options.why: It's understandable, but it guilt trips and puts Zoe in the message.

options.text: ok, guess we'll figure out another time. i'll tell her something came up
options.why: It leaves the next visit unclear and gives Zoe nothing to hold onto.

options.text: ok. do u want to call her at 7 tonight? next pickup is still sat at 10
options.why: It gives the kid a call and keeps the next date clear.

days.tryToday: If a visit falls through, offer one concrete thing for your kid, like a call at a set time.

days.title: "Just keep them then"
chat: Sometimes a schedule fight ends with them giving up the time: "just keep them then."
It can be a test, a guilt trip, or just a bad day. Usually it's hard to tell which.
It often helps to name the plan back calmly instead of grabbing the extra time or arguing.

options.text: great, i will then
options.why: It takes them up on it in a heated moment, which usually blows up later.

options.text: i know it's been a rough week. they're excited for ur wknd, see u fri at 5?
options.why: It's kind, names the plan and keeps the door open.

options.text: that's not what i said at all, i just asked if u could be on time for once on fridays
options.why: It reargues the last message instead of moving forward.

days.tryToday: When a text says "fine" or "whatever", answer with the next date and time and nothing else.

days.title: Long swaps for work
chat: Bigger changes, like a two-week work trip, need more detail than a quick swap.
Dates, times, who drives, and when the usual schedule picks back up.
Writing it all in one message saves five follow-ups.

them: so i got sent to denver for 2 wks in march
ill make it up to u w/ summer or something

options.text: yes. i'll take them march 3 to 17. can we swap 2 of ur summer weeks, which ones?
options.why: It says yes with the exact dates and pins down the make-up time.

options.text: yeah of course, no problem at all, we'll just figure out the summer stuff later on
options.why: It's generous, but "later" usually turns into a fight in June.

options.text: must be nice to just leave for 2 wks lol
options.why: It's a jab, and heated, when they asked for help.

days.tryToday: Next time you plan a long change, put the start date, end date and make-up time in one message.

days.title: Snow days and sick days
chat: Some changes nobody plans: school closes, a kid gets sick, the roads are bad.
These are the moments to be quick and practical.
Say who has the kid, until when, and what happens to the regular time.

them: i cant miss work again. can u?

options.text: i always have to cover these, it's ur turn
options.why: It turns a quick fix into a who-does-more fight.

options.text: maybe? let me see how my morning goes
options.why: It sounds open but leaves them stuck with no answer.

options.text: yep, i'll pick them up at 7:30 tmrw and drop them back by 6
options.why: It solves it with times, fast.

days.tryToday: Decide now who covers the next surprise school closure, and send one line to settle it.

days.title: Get it in writing
chat: A change agreed on the phone or at the door is easy to remember two different ways.
A short follow-up text makes it real: "just confirming, Sun at 4 instead of 6."
It's not about catching anyone. It's so you both have the same plan.

them: like i said at pickup, im getting them at 4 sun not 6

options.text: i didn't forget, u never said 4. u said "maybe earlier"
options.why: It argues about what was said instead of settling it.

options.text: ok, confirming sunday at 4 at my place
options.why: It confirms the new time in writing, which ends the confusion.

options.text: hmm i don't remember that but ok i guess
options.why: It agrees but adds doubt, so it's likely to come up again.

days.tryToday: After your next spoken agreement, send one text that confirms the day and time.

days.title: Plan summer before spring
chat: Summer fights usually start because nobody wrote the dates down in time.
An early message with specific weeks gives both of you room to plan.
That's the schedule module done. Next up: new partners.

them: have u thought about summer at all
or am i doing it all again

options.text: yep. i'd like july 5-19 for my two weeks. what weeks work for u?
options.why: It skips the jab and names real dates with a question back.

options.text: not yet, it's only february lol
options.why: It brushes it off, so the planning lands on them after all.

options.text: u do it all? i planned the whole thing last year, the camp, the beach week, all of it
options.why: It answers the jab and starts a fight about last year.

days.tryToday: Write down the weeks you'd like this summer, even if you don't send them yet.

days.title: When you hear about a new partner
chat: This module is new partners. Theirs or yours, it's one of the hardest topics to text about.
Often you hear about it from the kids first. That stings.
If you want to know something, ask about the part that affects the kids. Who they meet, when, and how.
Their love life isn't what you're answering. The kids' week is.

them: so the kids told me about "derek"
cool that i had to hear it from a 7 yr old
how long has that been going on

options.text: it's not that serious, i was going to tell u, it just never came up
options.why: It explains your timing, which gives them a fresh thing to argue about.

options.text: not that it's any of ur business but 3 months
options.why: It's a jab, and it turns the kids' news into a fight about you.

options.text: fair point. he's met the kids twice, always w/ me there. want to meet him?
options.why: It owns the one fair point and answers what matters for the kids.

days.tryToday: Think of one thing about a new partner that really affects the kids, and how you'd say it in one line.

days.title: "I want to meet them"
chat: It's common for a parent to want to meet someone who spends time with their kids.
You don't have to agree to every ask, but a calm answer with a next step keeps it from becoming a standoff.
Keep it about the kids: when, where, and how you'll handle it.

them: before she spends another wknd w/ MY kids

options.text: that's fair. could u meet her for coffee next week, maybe tues at 6?
options.why: It agrees and offers a time, so it's a plan, not a fight.

options.text: ok, she'll just stay away when the kids are here then, i don't want this to turn into a thing
options.why: It gives up something big just to avoid the conversation.

options.text: u don't get to make demands about who i date
options.why: It argues about rights instead of answering the ask.

days.tryToday: If you're open to an intro, write one line offering a day and a place.

days.title: When their partner texts you
chat: Sometimes the new partner reaches out directly. It can be friendly, or it can feel like a lot.
You can be polite and short, and keep the logistics with the parent.
Nobody has to be best friends. Calm is enough.

them: Hi! This is Jess, Mike's gf 😊
I'll be picking up the girls friday since he's working late

options.text: ok but i'd rather not get texts from u, pls have mike text me
options.why: It's cold to someone who was being polite, and it's about you, not pickup.

options.text: hi jess, thx for the heads up. they get out at 3:15 at the front door
options.why: It's friendly, short and gives the one thing she needs.

options.text: hi! omg thank u so much, we should get coffee sometime and talk about the girls!
options.why: It's warm, but it opens a whole new channel nobody planned.

days.tryToday: Decide what you'd say if a new partner ever texted you, in one line.

days.title: The partner at handoffs
chat: A new partner showing up at the handoff can feel like a lot, fast.
If it bothers you, ask about it as a plan, not a feeling about the person.
And if it's your partner, think about whether showing up helps the kids that day.

them: why is HE at every pickup now

options.text: because he's part of my life now. get used to it
options.why: It's defiant and invites a bigger fight.

options.text: ok fine, he'll stay home from now on, i didn't realize it bothered u that much
options.why: It gives in quickly, then you'll probably resent it.

options.text: ok. how about he waits in the car at pickups for now? see u fri at 5
options.why: It offers a small change and keeps the handoff on track.

days.tryToday: Picture your next handoff and decide who really needs to be there.

days.title: What the kids call them
chat: Hearing your kid call someone else "mom" or "dad" can really hurt.
If it comes up, talk to the other parent about it calmly and without blaming the kid.
Kids are usually just trying to fit into two homes.

them: so now isaac calls her MOM??
did u put him up to that

options.text: i didn't, i was surprised too. i'll tell him he can call her by her name
options.why: It's honest, calm, and offers a fix.

options.text: he can call her what he wants, he's a kid
options.why: It brushes off what's obviously painful for them.

options.text: ok i'll tell him to stop, i'm sorry, i should've caught it
options.why: It takes the blame for something that probably wasn't your doing.

days.tryToday: If it ever comes up, practise one line that doesn't blame your kid.

days.title: When they jab about you dating
chat: Comments about your dating life usually aren't questions. They're hooks.
There's no reply that makes them approve, so you don't need one.
If there's a logistics line in there, answer only that.

them: heard ur on tinder now lol
hope the kids arent ur second priority

options.text: i'm not on tinder, and the kids are always first, u know that
options.why: It defends you and gives them a new topic.

options.text: yep, sunday at 4 still works
options.why: It answers the real question and skips the rest.

options.text: at least someone wants to date me lol
options.why: It bites back and keeps the fight going.

days.tryToday: Next time a dating jab lands, find the logistics line and answer just that.

days.title: When their partner disciplines the kids
chat: A new partner telling your kid off can feel like a line was crossed.
Ask the parent, not the partner, with the specific thing that happened.
A clear ask beats a general complaint.

them: ethan said ur bf took his switch away for a week

options.text: he's an adult in the house and he's allowed to have rules, the kids need structure
options.why: It defends the partner and turns it into a fight about him.

options.text: ok i'll tell him to stay out of it
options.why: It agrees fast without saying what happened or what changes.

options.text: fair. i'll handle consequences myself from now on. ethan gets it back sat
options.why: It takes the point and gives a clear plan.

days.tryToday: Write down one rule you'd like both homes to agree on, so it isn't a surprise.

days.title: When your partner wants to defend you
chat: Your partner may want to jump into the thread to defend you. They mean well.
A third person in the conversation usually adds heat, not calm.
Keep the thread between the two parents, and thank your partner for caring.
replies: What do I tell my partner?

them: and tell ur gf to stop texting me
i dont need her opinion on my parenting

options.text: ok, i'll ask her not to. anything about the kids can come straight to me
options.why: It agrees and keeps the thread to the two of you.

options.text: she was just trying to help, u don't have to be so rude to her, she's never done anything to u
options.why: It defends her and grows the fight.

options.text: she's allowed to text whoever she wants
options.why: It's calm in tone but refuses something reasonable.

days.tryToday: If your partner wants to help, give them a role that isn't texting your co-parent.

days.title: Moving in together
chat: Moving in with someone is big news for the kids. Telling the other parent first is usually kinder.
Facts help: when, where, and anything that changes for the kids.
You don't need their blessing, just a clear heads-up.

them: so im hearing ur moving in w/ him
were u going to tell me
or just let the kids drop it on me

options.text: yeah sorry i meant to say something, it just happened fast and things have been busy
options.why: It explains and apologises but gives no facts.

options.text: yes, from march 1. same school, same schedule, kids get their own rooms
options.why: It gives the facts that matter for the kids.

options.text: why do u care? u don't live w/ us
options.why: It's defensive and starts a new fight.

days.tryToday: If you have big news, write the facts for the kids in one message before they hear it elsewhere.

days.title: Keep it on the kids
chat: The thread through this whole module: answer what affects the kids, and leave the rest.
Their feelings about your partner are real, but text can't fix them.
That's new partners done. Next up: holidays and birthdays.

them: ngl it hurts seeing her at noras games
can she just sit somewhere else

options.text: it's not about u, she just likes coming to watch nora play, she's really into soccer now
options.why: It's calm, but it brushes off the feeling and changes nothing.

options.text: honestly u need to get over it, it's been 2 years
options.why: It's cold and turns a hard moment into a fight.

options.text: that's fair. we'll sit on the other side so nora can see both of us
options.why: It hears them and makes a small change for Nora.

days.tryToday: Pick one small thing you could do so the kids feel less caught between two new lives.

days.title: Plan it before it's close
chat: This module is holidays and birthdays. Big feelings, small windows of time.
The closer the day gets, the hotter the texts get.
One early message with dates and handoff times takes a lot of the heat out.

them: are we doing the split thing again or what

options.text: yep, same as last year? u have them till 2, i pick up at 2 at ur place
options.why: It names the plan and the handoff time, weeks early.

options.text: idk yet, let's just figure it out closer to it when we know everyone's plans
options.why: It pushes it off to the week when everyone's stressed.

options.text: "the split thing" was ur idea btw
options.why: It argues about whose idea it was instead of planning.

days.tryToday: Look at the next holiday on the calendar and draft one line with the day and handoff time.

days.title: Splitting the day
chat: Splitting a holiday means a handoff in the middle of it, which is a lot of driving and a lot of feelings.
The calmest version is simple: a time, a place, and no comments on whose turn is better.
If the time isn't working, offer a new one instead of a complaint.

them: my moms flying in and the kids havent seen her since july

options.text: no, 2 is the plan, we agreed on it in october
options.why: It's firm but shuts the door on a fair ask with no option.

options.text: ugh fine. i guess my family just eats without them
options.why: It says yes with a guilt trip attached.

options.text: 5 works if i get them by 10am christmas eve. ok?
options.why: It says yes and trades fairly for something else.

days.tryToday: If a holiday time doesn't work, write a counter-offer with a specific time, not a complaint.

days.title: One party or two
chat: Birthday parties are a classic co-parenting spot. One party, two, who invites who.
There's no right answer, but there is a calm way to ask.
Say what you're thinking, keep it about the kid, and ask what they'd like.

them: r u planning ur own again
bc last year she was exhausted

options.text: i mean she has two homes, so she gets two parties
options.why: It's a fair point said like a jab, and it shuts down the question.

options.text: could we do one party together this year? i'm happy to split costs and planning
options.why: It offers a joint plan and invites them in.

options.text: ok i won't do one then
options.why: It gives up the party without a conversation.

days.tryToday: Write down what you'd like for your kid's next birthday, and one way you could share it.

days.title: When gifts become a contest
chat: Gifts can turn into a quiet competition. Who got the bigger one, who got the thing first.
If it stings, keep the reply about the kid having a good day.
A short check-in on big gifts can help next time.

them: so u got owen the bike
the bike I told u i was getting him

options.text: that's on me, i forgot. want to tell me what ur getting next time so we don't overlap?
options.why: It owns the slip and sets up a simple fix.

options.text: u never said that
options.why: It denies and starts a "you said, I said" fight.

options.text: omg it's a BIKE, he's happy, who cares 🙄
options.why: It's heated and brushes off a real feeling.

days.tryToday: Before the next big gift, send one line saying what you're planning.

days.title: Mother's Day and Father's Day
chat: These days can be hard when you're apart.
If the plan gives the day to one parent, a quick heads-up about the time helps.
And helping the kids make a card for the other parent is a kind thing, not a defeat.

them: is sunday still mine for mothers day
or do u have something "special" planned again

options.text: i don't have anything planned, why would u assume that? u always think i'm up to something
options.why: It answers the jab and skips the question.

options.text: yeah i guess, if u want
options.why: It sounds unsure, so the plan feels shaky.

options.text: yep, sunday's yours. i'll drop them off at 9 w/ a card they made
options.why: It confirms the day, the time and adds something kind.

days.tryToday: Help your kid make or send something for the other parent's day.

days.title: Holiday travel
chat: Traveling with the kids over a holiday needs a few details: where, when, and how to reach them.
Some parenting plans say something about travel. If yours does, follow it, and if you're unsure what it means, that's a question for a lawyer, not the thread.
By text, keep it to the facts.

options.text: it's my holiday week, i don't need ur permission
options.why: It argues permission instead of giving the details they asked for.

options.text: dec 26 to 30 at my sister's, 214 oak st. they can call u every night at 7
options.why: It gives the dates, the place and a call time.

options.text: just a few days, it's honestly no big deal, they'll be totally fine, i'll send pics
options.why: It's vague, which makes them more worried.

days.tryToday: If you're traveling with the kids, write the dates, the address and a call time in one text.

days.title: Halloween and the small holidays
chat: Small holidays can cause big fights, partly because they're not always in the plan.
A quick, specific offer works well: a time window and a place.
Kids remember the night, not who had them.

them: its my night but sofia wants to trick or treat w/ her friends on ur street
idk how u want to do this

options.text: want to bring her over at 6? she can go w/ her friends, u grab her at 8
options.why: It makes a clear plan around what Sofia wants.

options.text: she can just do it at ur house, it's fine
options.why: It's easy-going but ignores what Sofia actually wants.

options.text: i mean if it's ur night it's ur problem
options.why: It's calm in tone but unhelpful and a little cold.

days.tryToday: Think of one small holiday coming up and what a simple plan for it would be.

days.title: Grandparents and family
chat: Extended family wants time too. Sometimes that pulls on the schedule.
Ask for what you'd like, with a day and a time, and keep the family drama out of it.
Saying no to family time is allowed, and so is a counter-offer.

them: my parents want the kids for the 4th
its ur day but they're old and wont be around forever

options.text: that's a guilt trip and u know it
options.why: It names the guilt trip, which starts a fight about it.

options.text: ok they can have them, i'll do something else that day, i don't want to fight about it
options.why: It gives up the day just because of the guilt.

options.text: how about they come to my bbq that afternoon? or they can have them the 5th
options.why: It offers two real options without arguing.

days.tryToday: Write one sentence you could use to offer family time on a day that isn't the holiday itself.

days.title: The birthday on their day
chat: Sometimes your kid's birthday falls on the other parent's day.
A short ask for a call or a quick visit is reasonable. Make it easy to say yes.
And if the answer is no, plan your own celebration on your day.

them: hey just fyi maya's bday is on my wknd this year

options.text: so i don't even get to see her on her birthday? nice
options.why: It's sarcastic and skips the chance to ask for something.

options.text: sounds fun. can i call her at 7 on her bday? i'll do cake w/ her on mon
options.why: It's warm and asks for one easy thing.

options.text: ok that's fine, i'll just skip it this year
options.why: It gives up more than you needed to.

days.tryToday: If your kid's birthday is on the other parent's day, plan one call and your own celebration.

days.title: The last-minute holiday change
chat: Late changes over the holidays are stressful. Flights get moved, people get sick.
When it happens, answer the change with a new time, not a recap of the whole year.
That's the holidays module done. Next up: school and health decisions.

them: i need them back by 4 tn not 7

options.text: ok, i'll have them at ur place by 4. safe travels
options.why: It answers fast with the new time and a kind word.

options.text: ugh, that cuts our day short, can u see if there's a later flight?
options.why: It pushes back on something they probably can't change.

options.text: of course, plans always change around u
options.why: It turns a small change into a bigger fight.

days.tryToday: When the next plan changes, reply with the new time first, before anything else.

days.title: Big decisions by text
chat: This module is school and health. These are real decisions, not just logistics.
Text works for sharing information. It's a hard place to make a big decision.
Share the facts, say what you think, and suggest a call or a meeting if it's big.

them: i want to move eli to lincoln next year
the class sizes at his school are insane

options.text: no way, he's finally settled there
options.why: It shuts it down without any discussion.

options.text: sure, whatever u think is best
options.why: It gives up your say in a big decision.

options.text: open to it. can we tour lincoln together next month and decide after?
options.why: It's open, and puts the decision where it belongs.

days.tryToday: Pick one bigger decision coming up and write one line suggesting a time to talk about it.

days.title: Parent-teacher conferences
chat: At school, the kid is the topic. Not the other parent.
If you both go, sit together or apart, whatever keeps it calm.
If only one can go, share the notes after. Short and factual.

them: r u coming or do i have to take notes for u again

options.text: yes, i'll be there at 4:15. see u there
options.why: It confirms and skips the jab.

options.text: i've never asked u to take notes for me
options.why: It argues the jab and skips the answer.

options.text: i'll try to make it, depends on work
options.why: It's vague, so they don't know if you'll come.

days.tryToday: Ask the school if both parents can get emails and updates directly.

days.title: When you disagree on medicine
chat: Health disagreements are some of the most stressful texts.
By text, the most useful thing is usually to suggest asking the doctor together.
You don't need to win the medical argument. That's the doctor's area.

them: the dr wants to start zoe on meds for her focus
i dont want her drugged up

options.text: she needs it, ur just in denial
options.why: It's harsh and makes the decision harder.

options.text: i hear u. can we both go to her next appt and ask the dr our questions?
options.why: It hears them and suggests asking the doctor together.

options.text: ok, we won't start anything then. i'll tell the doctor we decided to wait for now
options.why: It drops a medical question without talking to the doctor.

days.tryToday: If there's a health question, write down your questions for the next doctor visit.

days.title: Counseling for the kids
chat: Sometimes one parent wants the kid to talk to a counselor, and the other doesn't.
It helps to keep it about the kid's needs and what you've noticed.
Parley isn't therapy and can't say what's right for your kid, but it can help you ask calmly.

them: why does ben need a therapist
bc i know ur family talks

options.text: honestly maybe it is, he's been really upset after ur weekends
options.why: It blames them and makes this about the adults.

options.text: no, it's not about u, i promise, i'm just worried
options.why: It reassures, but gives no detail about what's going on with Ben.

options.text: it's not about u. his teacher said he's been anxious. want to meet the counselor w/ me?
options.why: It shares what was noticed and invites them in.

days.tryToday: Write down one thing you've noticed about your kid lately, as a fact, not a judgment.

days.title: Haircuts, piercings, the small big things
chat: Some decisions seem small but feel big to the other parent: a haircut, a piercing, a phone.
A quick heads-up before, not after, avoids a lot of hurt.
If it already happened, a short honest reply works better than a defense.

options.text: fair. next time i'll check w/ u before anything like that
options.why: It owns it and sets up a better next time.

options.text: she really wanted it for her birthday and it's honestly just tiny earrings, not a big deal
options.why: It explains but doesn't respect the ask to be included.

options.text: ok and? u cut her hair last summer without asking me
options.why: It's a tit-for-tat that starts a whole new fight.

days.tryToday: Think of one small decision coming up and give a heads-up before it happens.

days.title: Injuries and urgent care
chat: When a kid gets hurt, the other parent wants to know fast.
Send the facts first: what happened, how they are, and where they are now.
The story of how it happened can wait.

them: why am i finding out on fb that harper broke her wrist

options.text: i was going to tell u, it's been a crazy day, it happened so fast at the trampoline park and
options.why: It's a long story that skips the facts they need.

options.text: she's ok, cast on, home now. ortho appt fri at 10, want to come?
options.why: It gives the facts and invites them in.

options.text: she's fine. relax
options.why: It's dismissive when they're scared.

days.tryToday: Save the pediatrician's number and your kid's insurance info somewhere both parents can find it.

days.title: When grades drop
chat: When grades slip, it's easy to blame the other house.
A plan helps more than a reason: what you'll each do, starting when.
Kids do better when both homes are on the same page, even loosely.

them: and dont tell me its not ur house bc his hw never gets done there

options.text: his hw gets done at my house, maybe check ur own first
options.why: It blames back and starts a fight.

options.text: ok i'll try to do better w/ it
options.why: It accepts the blame without a real plan.

options.text: i saw. can we both check his math hw each night? i'll email his teacher tmrw
options.why: It's a shared plan with a next step.

days.tryToday: Ask your kid's teacher one question by email this week.

days.title: Screens and phones
chat: Two homes often have two sets of screen rules.
You probably won't get identical rules, and that's ok.
Agree on one or two things that matter most, like bedtime phones.

them: chloe told me she's on her phone till midnight at ur place

options.text: fair. let's both say phones off at 9 on school nights?
options.why: It agrees with the worry and offers a shared rule.

options.text: she's exaggerating, it's like 10 at the latest and only on weekends really
options.why: It argues the detail and calls the kid a liar.

options.text: it's my house, my rules
options.why: It shuts down a reasonable worry.

days.tryToday: Pick one screen rule you'd like both homes to share and write it in one line.

days.title: Doctor visits and checkups
chat: Regular appointments are easy to share and easy to forget to share.
Send the date, the time, and what the doctor said after.
A quick summary keeps both parents in the loop without a debate.

them: did u take noras to the dentist

options.text: i didn't forget, they canceled on me
options.why: It argues the jab without a plan for the appointment.

options.text: they had to move it, it's now 10/14 at 3:30. i'll take her and send u the notes
options.why: It gives the new date, who's taking her and a follow-up.

options.text: can u just take her then, if they're calling u
options.why: It hands it off without saying when the appointment is.

days.tryToday: After your kid's next appointment, send the other parent a two-line summary.

days.title: Sharing the paperwork
chat: Report cards, school portals, medical records. Both parents usually want access.
Sharing it without being asked is a small thing that builds trust.
That's the school and health module done. Next up: kids caught in the middle.

them: can u send me the login for the school portal

options.text: u can call the school and get ur own login
options.why: It's true but unhelpful, and it reads as a brush-off.

options.text: ok i'll look for it when i'm home tonight, i think it's written down somewhere
options.why: It says yes but gives no time, after two asks already.

options.text: sending it now. i'll ask the school to set up ur own login too
options.why: It sends it right away and fixes the problem for next time.

days.tryToday: Send one piece of school or health info to the other parent without being asked.

days.title: When the kid asks why
chat: This module is about the kids caught between two homes.
When a kid asks "why don't you love dad anymore", what you say matters a lot.
Simple, honest, and never about blame. It's not their job to understand the adult stuff.

them: ruby asked me tonight why u dont love me anymore

options.text: nothing like that. i'll tell her we both love her and that grown-up stuff isn't her job
options.why: It reassures and keeps Ruby out of the adult stuff.

options.text: i don't know where she got that, maybe from ur sister?
options.why: It guesses at blame and starts a new fight.

options.text: well, it's kind of the truth, isn't it
options.why: It's cold and puts the adult fight into the kid's head.

days.tryToday: If your kid asks about the divorce, practise one line that says you both love them.

days.title: When the kid carries a demand
chat: Kids get used as messengers. "Mom says you have to pay for my camp."
Answer the other parent directly, and tell your kid it's not their job to carry messages.
Keep it light with the kid and clear with the adult.

them: ava told u about the camp thing right
so can u send ur half

options.text: yeah she told me, and i didn't love her being the one to tell me
options.why: It's fair but turns into a complaint, not an answer.

options.text: yep, saw the camp info. i'll send my $200 half fri. let's keep money stuff between us
options.why: It answers the money and asks to keep it adult-to-adult.

options.text: why are u making her ask me for money? that's so messed up
options.why: It's heated and turns it into a fight.

days.tryToday: Next time a kid passes a message, check it directly with the other parent.

days.title: Texting through the kid's phone
chat: Some parents text the kid when they want to reach the other parent.
It puts a lot on the kid's shoulders.
Answer directly yourself and gently suggest texting you for logistics.

them: i texted jayden to tell u im picking him up at 4 instead

options.text: he's 10, of course he forgot. why would u tell him and not me, that makes no sense
options.why: It's a fair point said with a bite, which starts a fight.

options.text: ok
options.why: It's a bare ok, which leaves the actual plan unclear.

options.text: he did, 4 works. next time just text me for pickups so he doesn't have to remember
options.why: It confirms the plan and gently asks to keep it between adults.

days.tryToday: Next time you need to change a plan, text the other parent, not the kid.

days.title: When the kid doesn't want to go
chat: Sometimes a kid doesn't want to go to the other home. It's hard on everyone.
Share what's happening, calmly, without making it a verdict on the other parent.
If there's a pattern, keep notes, and if you have a lawyer, that's who to ask about it.

them: liam says he doesnt want to come this wknd
did u tell him to say that

options.text: no. he said he's nervous about missing his friend's party sat. could he go at 2?
options.why: It answers honestly and offers a fix for the actual reason.

options.text: maybe he just doesn't want to be at ur place
options.why: It's cruel to them and puts Liam in the middle.

options.text: ok i'll make him go, don't worry
options.why: It forces it without hearing what's going on with Liam.

days.tryToday: If your kid ever says they don't want to go, ask them one gentle question about why before deciding anything.

days.title: When the kid repeats something cruel
chat: Your kid comes home and repeats something mean the other parent said about you.
It hurts. And your kid is watching how you react.
With your kid, stay calm and kind. With the other parent, you can ask them to keep it out of the kids' ears.
replies: What do I tell my kid?

them: max says u called me a deadbeat in front of him

options.text: i never said that, he's making stuff up, he does that when he's tired after ur place
options.why: It calls Max a liar and gives the other parent nothing.

options.text: i'll talk w/ max. let's both keep stuff about each other out of their ears
options.why: It handles the kid and asks for a shared rule.

options.text: well if the shoe fits
options.why: It's mean and proves the kid right.

days.tryToday: If your kid repeats something mean, tell them it's not their job to carry grown-up stuff.

days.title: Secrets between homes
chat: Asking kids to keep secrets from the other parent puts them in a tough spot.
If you find out your kid was asked to keep something from you, ask the other parent directly.
And skip asking your kid to keep secrets yourself.

them: emma said u told her not to tell me about the move
why would u make her keep that from me

options.text: i didn't tell her that, she must've misunderstood
options.why: It denies and leaves the news unshared.

options.text: why do u always assume the worst about me
options.why: It's defensive and skips the real question.

options.text: we're moving june 1, same school district. i'll tell u big stuff first from now on
options.why: It owns it and gives the facts.

days.tryToday: Notice one time this week you're tempted to say "don't tell your mom" or "don't tell your dad."

days.title: "Who do you want to live with?"
chat: Asking a kid to choose between parents puts a heavy weight on them.
If the other parent is asking, you can ask them to stop, calmly and briefly.
It's okay to tell your kid that grown-ups make that decision.

them: owen said he wants to live w/ me full time
so i think we need to talk about that

options.text: i'd like to hear what's going on w/ him. can we talk sun at 7, just us?
options.why: It's open and sets a time to talk away from Owen.

options.text: he said the exact same thing to me last week, so i think he's just telling us both what we want to hear
options.why: It turns it into a contest over who Owen picked.

options.text: ok if that's what he wants
options.why: It gives up a big decision in one line.

days.tryToday: If your kid brings it up, practise saying that grown-ups decide and both homes love them.

days.title: Stuff that doesn't travel
chat: A favorite toy, a game console, a soccer jersey that never comes back.
It can feel like a power play. Often it's just forgotten.
Ask for the item, give a time, and keep it about the kid's needs.

them: isaac left his switch at ur place
can u bring it or is he just not getting it back

options.text: he can just play it here, it's fine
options.why: It ignores that Isaac wants it at both homes.

options.text: yep, i'll drop it off tmrw at 5
options.why: It answers with a time.

options.text: omg it's not a hostage situation lol
options.why: It's heated and mocking.

days.tryToday: Next time something's forgotten, reply with when you'll drop it off and nothing else.

days.title: When they overheard
chat: Kids overhear calls, see texts, notice tone. They hear more than we think.
If a kid overheard a fight, talk to them about it simply: grown-ups argue sometimes, and it's not their fault.
With the other parent, agree to keep heated talks away from the kids.
replies: What do I tell my kid?

them: noah heard us on the phone last night
he asked me if we're going to court

options.text: u were the one yelling, not me
options.why: It's blame, and it starts round two.

options.text: ok, he'll be fine, kids hear stuff all the time. i wouldn't worry about it too much
options.why: It brushes off something that really matters to Noah.

options.text: i'll talk w/ him tonight. let's only have calls after he's asleep from now on?
options.why: It handles Noah and suggests a simple rule.

days.tryToday: Pick a time for hard calls when the kids are asleep or out of the house.

days.title: They're kids, not couriers
chat: The thread through this module: kids aren't messengers, judges or spies.
When news comes through them, take it to the adult. When feelings come through them, take care of the kid.
That's kids in the middle done. Next up: old fights dragged up.

them: mia says ur new place is tiny lol
and that she sleeps on a couch

options.text: she has her own room, it's small but it's hers. want me to send u a pic?
options.why: It answers the fact and offers to show it.

options.text: she's 7, she says lots of stuff
options.why: It brushes off the question and dismisses Mia.

options.text: lol u live in an apartment too, stop
options.why: It's a jab, and it's heated.

days.tryToday: Next time a kid shares news about the other home, check it with the adult before reacting.

days.title: The midnight essay
chat: This module is old fights. The ones that show up in the middle of a pickup text.
Sometimes they arrive as one huge message late at night.
Read it once, find the one real ask buried in it, and answer only that. In the morning, if you can.

them: honestly i cant sleep bc i keep thinking about how u checked out years before u left and i held everything together
and now ur dad of the year. anyway can u get them at 3 tmrw instead of 5

options.text: i didn't check out, i was working 60 hour weeks for this family and u know it
options.why: It answers the history and skips the one question.

options.text: i'm sorry u feel that way, i know it was hard for u too. we both made mistakes and i think
options.why: It's kind, but it opens the old fight up again at midnight.

options.text: yes, i'll get them at 3 tmrw
options.why: It answers the one real ask and lets the rest go.

days.tryToday: If a long late-night message comes in, wait till morning and answer only the ask.

days.title: When the affair comes up
chat: The biggest hurts tend to come up in the smallest texts.
A logistics question can arrive wrapped in "you cheated" or "you left".
You don't need to defend or confess by text. Answer the plan, and keep the rest for a different room, if anywhere.

them: u want the kids for easter after what u did?

options.text: i'd like to get them at 10 on easter sunday and bring them back at 6
options.why: It answers the time and lets the rest go.

options.text: we've been over this so many times, i've said i'm sorry, i don't know what else u want from me
options.why: It reopens the hurt instead of answering the plan.

options.text: ok, u can have easter if that's easier
options.why: It gives up the day out of guilt.

days.tryToday: Next time the past is the opener, look for the question at the end and answer that.

days.title: Old money grudges
chat: Money fights from the marriage tend to show up years later.
"You still owe me for the car." "You emptied the account."
Old money stuff is rarely settled by text. Keep today's money about today.

them: ur asking ME for daycare money
after u drained the savings account in 2021

options.text: i didn't drain it, half of that money was mine and u know it
options.why: It argues 2021 instead of this month's daycare.

options.text: this is just for march daycare, $640, ur half is $320. receipt attached
options.why: It keeps it to the one bill this month.

options.text: ok forget the daycare money then
options.why: It drops a fair ask to avoid an old fight.

days.tryToday: Next time old money comes up, answer only the current amount.

days.title: When they rewrite history
chat: Hearing someone retell the past wrong is maddening.
"You never helped when they were babies." You want to correct it with the receipts.
But a text won't change their memory. It just keeps the old fight alive.

them: funny how u want to be involved now
so can u pick ruby up from dance thurs or not

options.text: i changed plenty of diapers, ask ur mom, she saw me
options.why: It argues the past and brings in a witness.

options.text: that's not fair, i was there a lot more than u remember
options.why: It argues the past without answering the question.

options.text: yes, i'll pick ruby up from dance thursday at 6
options.why: It answers the real question.

days.tryToday: When the past is wrong in a text, let it be wrong, and answer the plan.

days.title: Anniversaries and hard dates
chat: Certain dates bring old fights back: the anniversary, the day someone moved out.
If you notice texts get hotter around a date, that's useful to know.
On those days, it can help to keep replies even shorter than usual.

them: anyway kids need lunch money tmrw

options.text: ok, i'll send lunch money w/ them tmrw
options.why: It's kind by being short and answering the ask.

options.text: i didn't forget, i just don't think it's worth bringing up
options.why: It answers the hurt with a sting.

options.text: i know, it's a hard day for me too. do u want to talk about it?
options.why: It's well meant, but it reopens the marriage on a hard day.

days.tryToday: Note the dates that tend to bring hot texts, so you're ready for them.

days.title: "Remember when you..."
chat: One old mistake can follow you around: the time you forgot pickup, the time you were late to the hospital.
Each time it comes back, you don't have to defend it again.
Answer today's ask, and let the old story be.

them: just making sure u dont forget her at school again

options.text: that was 4 yrs ago, can we let it go
options.why: It's a fair point, but it keeps the old story going.

options.text: got it, 2:45 early release. i'll be there
options.why: It confirms the time and skips the jab.

options.text: u've forgotten plenty of stuff too, want me to make a list?
options.why: It's a counter-attack.

days.tryToday: Next time an old mistake comes up, answer the plan only.

days.title: When they want an apology
chat: Sometimes they want you to say sorry for something from years ago.
It's your call whether to apologise. If you do, keep it short and honest, and not in the middle of a logistics fight.
If you don't, you can still answer the plan.

them: ill sign the camp form when u admit what u did

options.text: fine, i'm sorry for everything, ok? i was wrong about all of it. can u just sign the form now
options.why: It apologises under pressure, which rarely lands as real.

options.text: that's blackmail and u know it
options.why: It names it, which starts a fight about it.

options.text: the camp form is due fri. i'll drop it off w/ the kids tmrw so u can sign it
options.why: It keeps the form separate from the past.

days.tryToday: Keep the logistics separate from the past in your next tense text.

days.title: When their family joins in
chat: Sometimes the other parent's family brings up the old fights.
You don't have to answer them, and a quick kind no is usually enough.
Keep the co-parenting talk with the co-parent.

them: I think you owe my son an explanation for how you treated him.

options.text: hi linda. i'll keep things about the kids between jake and me. take care
options.why: It's polite, short and closes the door gently.

options.text: with all due respect, u don't know what happened in our marriage
options.why: It invites a debate with someone outside the co-parenting.

options.text: i'm sorry u feel that way, linda. i've always tried my best
options.why: It's polite but invites more back and forth.

days.tryToday: If extended family texts you, write one polite line that sends it back to the co-parent.

days.title: When you want to bring it up
chat: It's not always them. Sometimes you're the one who wants to drag up the past.
If you're writing a text with "remember when" in it, pause.
Ask yourself: will this get the kids what they need this week?

options.text: sure, like u did for me every time i asked during the divorce? oh wait
options.why: It's a polite-looking dig from the past.

options.text: yep, i'll take them tues. pickup from school at 3?
options.why: It answers the ask, nothing extra.

options.text: yes but this is the 3rd time and i'm keeping track
options.why: It says yes with a warning that starts a fight.

days.tryToday: Catch one draft this week where you were about to bring up the past, and cut it.

days.title: Let the past stay past
chat: The thread through this module: old fights can't be won by text.
You can answer the current question and let the rest be.
That's old fights done. Next up: threats and "see you in court."

them: ur doing the same thing u did when we were married
r u taking them to the lake or not

options.text: yes, sat 9 to 5 at lake tahoma w/ my sister. want the address?
options.why: It answers the question and gives the details.

options.text: i'm not doing the same thing at all, that's so unfair, i told u about the lake last week
options.why: It defends you and skips the answer.

options.text: i don't have to ask u about my weekend
options.why: It's true-ish, but cold, and it skips the question.

days.tryToday: Next time you see the past in a text, find the question and answer only that.

days.title: "See you in court"
chat: This module is threats. The texts that make your stomach drop.
Parley can't tell you what a threat means legally. If you have a lawyer, they're the one to ask.
What we can practise is the reply: don't threaten back, don't argue the law by text, answer the plan, and save the message.

them: keep it up and ill see u in court

options.text: go ahead, my lawyer is better than urs
options.why: It's a counter-threat and keeps the fight going.

options.text: ok. pickup is still fri at 5 at school
options.why: It doesn't argue and keeps to the plan.

options.text: please don't do that, we can work this out, i'll do whatever u want
options.why: It gives up everything out of fear.

days.tryToday: Save the next threat you get to your record, without replying to it right away.

days.title: "My lawyer says"
chat: Sometimes the other parent quotes their lawyer in a text.
You don't have to argue what their lawyer said, and you don't have to agree either.
If it's about a legal question, that's one for your own lawyer if you have one.
replies: What if I don't have a lawyer?

them: my lawyer says u cant take them out of the county

options.text: ur lawyer is wrong, i checked and i can
options.why: It argues the law by text, which rarely helps.

options.text: ok i'll cancel it i guess, if that's what ur lawyer says. i don't want any trouble
options.why: It gives up the plan based on something nobody has checked.

options.text: ok. i'll check w/ my own lawyer and get back to u by fri
options.why: It doesn't argue and gives a time for a real answer.

days.tryToday: If a legal question comes up, write it down for a lawyer instead of debating it by text.

days.title: Threats to keep the kids
chat: "You won't see them this weekend." It's one of the scariest texts.
Don't match it. Answer with the plan you have, the time and the place.
Save the message. If you have a lawyer, that's who to tell.

them: ur not getting them this wknd
i dont care what the schedule says

options.text: i'll be at the usual spot sat at 10 like the schedule says
options.why: It states the plan, calmly.

options.text: u can't do that, i'll call the cops
options.why: It's a counter-threat in a hot moment.

options.text: ok, i'll wait till ur ready. just let me know when i can see them again i guess
options.why: It gives up the time without a word.

days.tryToday: Save one message that worried you to your record, with the date.

days.title: Threats to report you
chat: Some threats are about calling the police or child services.
It's scary, especially when there's nothing to report.
Stay calm, don't argue, keep the reply about the kids. And if anyone is ever in danger, call emergency services right away.

them: the kids said u leave them alone all the time

options.text: go ahead, they'll see ur the problem
options.why: It's a counter-attack and doesn't help.

options.text: please don't, i'm begging u, i didn't do anything
options.why: It pleads, which gives the threat more power.

options.text: the kids are never home alone. if ur worried, let's talk sun at 7
options.why: It states the fact calmly and offers a talk.

days.tryToday: Write down who you'd call first if a threat like this came in.

days.title: Threats to move away
chat: "I'm moving to Texas with the kids." A big threat in a few words.
What a move means depends on your plan and where you live, so that's a lawyer's question, not the thread's.
By text, ask for the facts, calmly.

options.text: over my dead body
options.why: It's a big reaction that won't help, and it's heated.

options.text: ok. can u send me the details, dates and where, so i can plan?
options.why: It asks for the facts without agreeing or arguing.

options.text: ok if that's what's best
options.why: It agrees to something huge in one line.

days.tryToday: If big news like this comes in, write down your questions before replying.

days.title: Threats to tell the kids
chat: "I'll tell them what you really did." Threats to turn the kids against you are some of the worst.
You can ask them, once and briefly, to keep the kids out of it.
Then keep doing what you do on your time. That's what the kids see.

them: maybe its time the kids knew the truth about u

options.text: let's keep the kids out of grown-up stuff. see u fri at 5
options.why: It asks once, calmly, and keeps the plan.

options.text: go ahead, tell them, they'll see who u really are
options.why: It's a dare, and it puts the kids in danger of hearing it.

options.text: please don't, i'll do anything, just tell me what u want me to do and i'll do it
options.why: It begs, which gives them power.

days.tryToday: Notice how you'd answer a threat like this, and practise keeping it to one line.

days.title: Threats to post online
chat: Some threats are about social media. "I'll put this all on Facebook."
Don't threaten back and don't argue about it. Answer once, and save it.
If kids' privacy is involved, keep the reply about the kids.

them: maybe ill just post the texts
let everyone see what kind of parent u are

options.text: do it, i'll post urs too
options.why: It's tit-for-tat, which escalates.

options.text: please don't, i'd be so embarrassed, my family and my work friends are all on there
options.why: It shows fear and gives them a lever.

options.text: i'd rather we keep the kids' stuff private. see u sat at 10
options.why: It asks once and stays on the plan.

days.tryToday: Read one of your recent texts as if a stranger were reading it, and see how it sounds.

days.title: "I'm screenshotting everything"
chat: When someone says they're screenshotting, it can feel like a trap.
It can also be a good reminder: anything you text might be read by someone else one day.
So write every text as if a calm stranger were reading it.

them: just so u know im screenshotting all of this
so be careful what u say

options.text: good, screenshot this then: ur the worst co-parent
options.why: It's a hot reply that ends up in the screenshot.

options.text: ok. pickup's still sun at 4
options.why: It's calm and on the plan.

options.text: wow ok, ur really doing this huh
options.why: It sounds calm but reads as a dig.

days.tryToday: Read your last three texts as if someone else were reading them, and notice how they'd sound.

days.title: When you want to threaten back
chat: It's normal to want to hit back when you're threatened.
But a counter-threat almost never makes things calmer.
Write the angry draft somewhere else if you need to, then send the calm one.

them: i'll make sure u never see them again

options.text: i'll see u fri at 5 for pickup like the schedule says
options.why: It skips the threat and states the plan.

options.text: try it and see what happens
options.why: It's a counter-threat, which escalates.

options.text: why would u say something like that to me
options.why: It's understandable, but it invites more.

days.tryToday: If you write an angry draft, write it in your notes app, not the chat.

days.title: Save it, don't fight it
chat: The thread through this module: threats are for saving and, if you have one, for your lawyer. Not for arguing.
Parley isn't a law firm and doesn't give legal advice. But a calm reply is always yours to send.
That's threats done. Last module: handoffs and in-person moments.

them: next time ur late im keeping them and calling my lawyer

options.text: and i'll call mine, see who wins
options.why: It's a counter-threat.

options.text: ok i'll never be late again, i promise
options.why: It promises something you can't guarantee, out of fear.

options.text: ok. i'll be there fri at 5
options.why: It answers the plan only.

days.tryToday: Save one threat to your record with a one-line note, then reply to the plan or not at all.

days.title: Picking the handoff spot
chat: The last module is handoffs: the moments where you're face to face, kids watching.
A good handoff spot is neutral, easy for both, and calm for the kids.
If the current spot isn't working, suggest a new one with a reason that's about the kids.

them: im not driving to ur place anymore

options.text: it's not my fault u moved so far
options.why: It argues about the move instead of solving the drive.

options.text: ok, halfway works. how about the target lot on route 9 at 5?
options.why: It agrees and names the spot and time.

options.text: ugh fine, i'll do all the driving then, even tho it's 40 min for me too
options.why: It says yes with a sigh and takes on all the work.

days.tryToday: If your handoff spot isn't working, write one line suggesting a specific new one.

days.title: When they start something at the car
chat: Sometimes the other parent starts a fight right at the handoff.
In person, the calm move is short: a nod, the kids' bags, a goodbye.
If they keep going, you can say "let's talk later" and leave. You don't have to win it in the parking lot.
replies: What do I say out loud?

them: and dont think i didnt see that
the way u looked at me at the car

options.text: ok. next handoff is wed at 5, see u then
options.why: It's short and on the plan.

options.text: i didn't look at u at all, ur imagining things
options.why: It argues something nobody can prove.

options.text: maybe if u didn't start stuff at the car
options.why: It's blame back.

days.tryToday: Plan what you'll say out loud at the next handoff, in one short line.

days.title: When the kid melts down
chat: Some kids cry or cling at handoffs. It's hard to watch.
It's not usually a sign that one home is bad. Transitions are just hard.
Calm and consistent helps most. Short goodbyes, a hug, and a plan.

them: zoe screamed the whole way home after u dropped her
she clearly doesnt want to be here

options.text: nothing, maybe it's ur house she doesn't want
options.why: It's a jab that hurts and doesn't help Zoe.

options.text: she's just tired, it's fine
options.why: It brushes off something real for both of them.

options.text: goodbyes have been hard for her lately. want to try a shorter handoff at the door?
options.why: It names it calmly and offers a fix.

days.tryToday: Try a shorter, calmer goodbye at your next handoff.

days.title: Forgotten stuff at handoff
chat: Backpacks, meds, homework. Things get left behind.
When it happens, it's a logistics question, not a character flaw.
Say when and how it'll get there. That's all.

options.text: and u forgot his jacket last week, so we're even
options.why: It keeps score instead of solving it.

options.text: i'll drop his glasses at school b4 8 tmrw
options.why: It fixes it with a time.

options.text: ugh i'm so sorry, i'm so scattered lately, i feel awful
options.why: It apologises too much and gives no fix.

days.tryToday: Make a short checklist for handoffs: meds, glasses, homework, chargers.

days.title: Running into each other at school
chat: School concerts, open houses, field days. You'll run into each other.
A simple "hi" and a focus on the kid is plenty.
You don't need to chat. You don't need to avoid each other either.

them: so are we sitting together at the concert or what
i dont want it to be weird for nora

options.text: i'm fine sitting near u. let's just say hi to her together after?
options.why: It keeps it simple and about Nora.

options.text: i'd rather not, honestly. i'll just sit in the back and find her after the show
options.why: It's honest but a bit cold, and leaves Nora's worry hanging.

options.text: it's only weird if u make it weird
options.why: It's a dig that makes it weirder.

days.tryToday: Decide how you'll say hi at the next school event, in one line.

days.title: Sitting near each other at games
chat: Games and recitals are where kids look up for both parents.
If you can, sit where they can see you both. If it's too tense, a different spot is fine.
Cheer for the kid, not the score in the stands.

them: can u not bring ur whole family to every game

options.text: they're the kid's family too, they can come
options.why: It's a fair point that turns into a fight.

options.text: ok they'll stop coming
options.why: It gives up family support for the kid.

options.text: ok, we'll sit on the other side so there's space. ben loves having them there
options.why: It makes space without giving anything up.

days.tryToday: At the next game, cheer for your kid and nothing else.

days.title: When they want to come in
chat: Sometimes the other parent wants to come inside at a handoff, or asks to come to your place.
You're allowed to keep handoffs at the door.
Say it kindly and plainly.

them: can i come in for a min when i drop them off
i want to see their rooms

options.text: no, ur not coming into my house
options.why: It's a sharp no with nothing kind in it.

options.text: i'd rather keep handoffs at the door for now. happy to send u pics of their rooms
options.why: It's a kind no with an option.

options.text: ok sure
options.why: It says yes when you'd rather not.

days.tryToday: Decide what your handoff boundary is, and write it in one line.

days.title: What you say out loud
chat: At handoffs, the kids hear every word.
"Have fun at dad's" or "see you Sunday" tells them it's ok to go.
Save the logistics for text, and keep the spoken part warm and short.

them: ella said u told her "good luck at ur moms" at pickup

options.text: i meant her spelling test. i'll say have fun next time
options.why: It explains in one line and offers a better phrase.

options.text: she's twisting my words, i said good luck w/ ur test and she knows that
options.why: It blames Ella.

options.text: it means what it means
options.why: It's cold and makes it worse.

days.tryToday: Pick a warm, short goodbye phrase to use at every handoff.

days.title: The text after a bad handoff
chat: After a tense handoff, the urge is to text about it right away.
Wait a bit. If you still need to say something, keep it about the next one.
One line, one fix, no recap.

options.text: it wouldn't be a mess if u didn't start it
options.why: It blames and starts round two.

options.text: i know, i'm sorry, i'll try harder
options.why: It takes all the blame without a plan.

options.text: agreed. how about we keep it to a quick hi and bags at the door next time?
options.why: It agrees and offers a simple plan.

days.tryToday: After the next tense handoff, wait an hour before you text about it.

days.title: Ninety days of practice
chat: That's the last of the nine modules. Ninety days of practice on top of the course.
The skills are the same ones you started with: pause, find the ask, keep it short, keep the kids out of it.
They hold best when you keep using them on real texts.
Thanks for showing up for this. It matters for your kids.

them: just wanted to say the kids seemed happy this wknd

options.text: thx, but let's see if it lasts
options.why: It turns a kind moment into a doubt.

options.text: thx, that's good to hear. they had a great time w/ u too
options.why: It's warm and returns the kindness.

options.text: thx. honestly it'd be nice if it was like this more often
options.why: It's a polite dig that spoils a kind moment.

days.tryToday: Notice one calm moment with the other parent this week, and say thanks for it.
